text: Which EU institution holds the right of legislative initiative in most policy areas?
explanation: The European Commission holds the near-exclusive right of legislative initiative under Article 17 TEU. The Parliament and Council can request proposals, but only the Commission can formally submit them.

text: How many Commissioners currently sit in the College of the European Commission?
explanation: The College of Commissioners has 27 members — one per EU Member State — each responsible for a specific policy area. The President decides the allocation of responsibilities.

text: What is the term of office of the European Commission?
explanation: The European Commission serves a 5-year term, aligned with the legislative term of the European Parliament. The current von der Leyen II Commission took office in December 2024.

text: Where does the European Parliament hold its plenary sessions?
explanation: The European Parliament holds its official plenary sessions in Strasbourg (France). Committee meetings and additional plenary sessions take place in Brussels. The General Secretariat is based in Luxembourg.

text: How many MEPs sit in the European Parliament for the 2024–2029 term?
explanation: The 2024–2029 European Parliament has 720 MEPs, an increase from 705 in the previous term. Seats are distributed among Member States using degressive proportionality.

text: Who presides over the European Council?
options: The elected President of the European Council
The Head of State of the rotating Presidency
The President of the European Commission
The High Representative for Foreign Affairs
explanation: The European Council has its own elected President (currently António Costa since December 2024), chosen by the European Council for a renewable 2.5-year term. This is distinct from the rotating Presidency of the Council of the EU.

text: How often does the European Council normally meet?
explanation: The European Council meets at least twice per semester (i.e. at least four times per year), normally in Brussels. The President may convene extraordinary meetings when required.

text: Which Council of the EU configuration is NOT chaired by the rotating Presidency?
explanation: The Foreign Affairs Council is chaired permanently by the High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, currently Kaja Kallas. All other Council configurations are chaired by the rotating six-month Presidency.

text: What percentage of Council members must vote in favour to reach a qualified majority?
explanation: Under the double majority rule (Lisbon Treaty), a qualified majority requires at least 55% of Member States (15 out of 27) representing at least 65% of the EU's total population. A blocking minority requires at least 4 states representing 35% of the population.

text: Where is the Court of Justice of the EU located?
explanation: The Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU) is located in Luxembourg. It comprises the Court of Justice, the General Court, and specialised courts. It is the judicial authority ensuring uniform interpretation of EU law.

text: Which procedure allows national courts to ask the CJEU to interpret EU law?
explanation: The preliminary reference procedure (Article 267 TFEU) allows national courts to refer questions on the interpretation or validity of EU law to the CJEU. Courts of last resort are obliged to refer; lower courts may do so voluntarily.

theme: Institutions - BCE et Cour des comptes
text: Where is the European Central Bank headquartered?
explanation: The European Central Bank (ECB) is headquartered in Frankfurt, Germany. Its primary objective is to maintain price stability in the euro area, with a symmetric 2% inflation target.

theme: Institutions - BCE et Cour des comptes
text: Which EU institution audits the revenue and expenditure of the EU?
explanation: The European Court of Auditors (ECA), seated in Luxembourg, audits all EU revenue and expenditure. It publishes an annual report and special reports on specific EU policies. It is one of the seven EU institutions.

text: Which landmark 1963 CJEU ruling established the principle of direct effect of EU law?
explanation: Van Gend en Loos (1963) established the principle of direct effect: EU law creates rights that individuals can invoke before national courts. Costa v ENEL (1964) established primacy. Francovich (1991) established State liability.

text: Which 1964 CJEU ruling established the primacy of EU law over national law?
explanation: Costa v ENEL (1964) established that EU law takes precedence over national law, including constitutions. This principle of primacy is not explicitly stated in the Treaties but derives from this founding case law.

text: Which type of EU legal act is directly applicable in all Member States without transposition?
explanation: A Regulation is directly applicable in all Member States as soon as it enters into force — no transposition into national law is required. A Directive binds Member States to achieve results but leaves the choice of method to national authorities.

text: Which EU legal instrument is binding on those to whom it is addressed but does not require transposition?
explanation: A Decision is binding in its entirety on those to whom it is addressed (which may be specific Member States, companies or individuals). Unlike a Directive, it does not require transposition into national law.

text: What is the name of the standard EU legislative procedure?
explanation: The Ordinary Legislative Procedure (OLP), introduced by the Lisbon Treaty, replaced the codecision procedure. It involves the Commission proposing, and the Parliament and Council co-deciding on an equal footing. About 80% of legislation passes at first reading via informal trilogues.

text: In the Ordinary Legislative Procedure, which institution formally introduces legislative proposals?
explanation: The European Commission holds the quasi-exclusive right of legislative initiative under Article 17 TEU. The Parliament and Council may request the Commission to propose legislation, but cannot themselves formally initiate it under the OLP.

text: What is a 'trilogue' in EU legislative practice?
options: Informal trilateral negotiation between Parliament, Council and Commission
A treaty between three EU institutions
A three-reading procedure in the Council
A joint committee of three MEPs and
explanation: A trilogue is an informal three-way negotiation between representatives of the European Parliament, the Council and the European Commission, aiming to reach agreement before the formal legislative readings. Today, about 80% of EU legislation is adopted at first reading via trilogues.

text: Which of the following is an exclusive competence of the EU?
explanation: The customs union is an exclusive EU competence (Article 3 TFEU): only the EU may act in this area. Environment and public health are shared or supporting competences. Education is a supporting competence where the EU may only coordinate.

text: Which policy area is a SHARED competence between the EU and Member States?
explanation: The internal market is a shared competence under Article 4 TFEU, meaning both the EU and Member States may legislate, but Member States may only act where the EU has not exercised its competence. Trade policy and monetary policy (euro) and the customs union are exclusive EU competences.

text: Under which EU principle does the Union only act if objectives cannot be sufficiently achieved by Member States alone?
explanation: The subsidiarity principle (Article 5 TEU) applies to non-exclusive competences: the EU may only act if the objectives of the proposed action cannot be sufficiently achieved at national, regional or local level, but can be better achieved at Union level.

text: When did the Treaty of Lisbon enter into force?
explanation: The Treaty of Lisbon entered into force on 1 December 2009, after ratification by all 27 Member States. It was signed on 13 December 2007. It amended the TEU and the Treaty of Rome (renamed TFEU).

text: Which article of the TEU provides the legal basis for a Member State to withdraw from the EU?
explanation: Article 50 TEU, introduced by the Lisbon Treaty, provides the procedure for a Member State to voluntarily leave the EU. It was first activated by the United Kingdom on 29 March 2017, leading to Brexit on 31 January 2020.

text: Which treaty established the European Economic Community?
explanation: The Treaty of Rome (25 March 1957) established the European Economic Community (EEC), which became the European Community under Maastricht and the basis for the current TFEU under the Lisbon Treaty.

text: Which treaty first introduced EU citizenship?
explanation: The Maastricht Treaty (1992) introduced EU citizenship for the first time. It is conferred automatically on every national of a Member State and complements, without replacing, national citizenship.

text: The Single European Act (1986) set a deadline for completing the internal market. What was that deadline?
explanation: The Single European Act (1986) set 1 January 1993 as the deadline for completing the internal market — a space without internal frontiers ensuring free movement of goods, persons, services and capital.

text: Which 1974 CJEU ruling made measures equivalent to quantitative trade restrictions illegal?
explanation: The Dassonville ruling (1974) established that any measure capable of hindering, directly or indirectly, intra-EU trade constitutes a measure of equivalent effect to a quantitative restriction, prohibited by the Treaty.

text: Which 1979 CJEU ruling established the principle of mutual recognition of goods?
explanation: Cassis de Dijon (1979) established mutual recognition: a product lawfully manufactured in one Member State must in principle be admitted to the market of any other Member State, unless the state can justify a restriction on overriding grounds of public interest.

text: How many Member States does the EU currently have?
explanation: Following the UK's withdrawal (Brexit, 31 January 2020), the EU has 27 Member States. The last country to join was Croatia on 1 July 2013.

text: Which country was the most recent to join the EU?
explanation: Croatia became the 28th (now 27th after Brexit) Member State on 1 July 2013. Bulgaria and Romania joined in 2007. North Macedonia is currently a candidate country.

text: How many EU Member States are in the euro area in 2024?
explanation: As of 2024, 20 EU Member States use the euro. Croatia became the 20th on 1 January 2023. Seven Member States have not yet adopted the euro (Sweden, Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, Denmark).

text: What is the primary objective of the European Central Bank?
explanation: The primary objective of the ECB is to maintain price stability (Article 127 TFEU), defined as keeping inflation close to, but below, 2% over the medium term (revised to a symmetric 2% target in 2021). Without prejudice to this objective, it supports the EU's general economic policies.

text: What are the Stability and Growth Pact's deficit and debt reference values?
explanation: The Stability and Growth Pact (1997) sets reference values of 3% of GDP for the general government deficit and 60% of GDP for public debt. Exceeding these values triggers the Excessive Deficit Procedure.

text: When was the European Stability Mechanism (ESM) established?
explanation: The ESM entered into force on 27 September 2012 as a permanent crisis resolution mechanism for the euro area. It replaced the temporary EFSF and EFSM. It can provide up to €700 billion in financial assistance to Member States.

text: What share of the EU's GDP does its annual budget approximately represent?
explanation: The EU budget represents approximately 1% of the EU's Gross National Income (GNI), far smaller than national budgets (typically 40-50% of GDP). The own resources ceiling is set at 1.4% of GNI for the 2021-2027 MFF period.

text: What is the total budget of the NextGenerationEU recovery instrument?
explanation: NextGenerationEU (NGEU), adopted in July 2020, amounts to €750 billion (in 2018 prices), financed through common EU borrowing. It includes the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) of €672.5 billion, supporting green and digital transitions post-COVID.

text: What is the EU's climate neutrality target under the European Climate Law?
explanation: The European Climate Law (2021) sets a legally binding EU-wide target of climate neutrality by 2050 and an intermediate target of at least 55% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared to 1990 levels.

text: What is the 'Fit for 55' package?
options: A social programme for workers aged 55+
A fund for the 55 poorest EU regions
An energy efficiency standard for buildings
A legislative package aligning with the EU's 55%
explanation: 'Fit for 55' is a set of legislative proposals to revise and update EU legislation to align with the goal of reducing net greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% by 2030. It covers the ETS, land use, renewable energy, energy efficiency, transport, and carbon border adjustment.

text: What does the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) primarily regulate?
options: Fines on Member States exceeding emissions targets
Taxes on fossil fuels for household consumers
A cap-and-trade system limiting CO2 emissions
explanation: The EU ETS is the world's largest carbon market, operating since 2005. It sets a cap on total greenhouse gas emissions from covered sectors (power, heavy industry, aviation). Companies must hold allowances for each tonne of CO2 emitted and can trade them.

text: What does the EU's Digital Services Act (DSA) primarily address?
options: Licensing of digital services in the
Digital skills training for public sector workers
Obligations of platforms regarding illegal and harmful content
explanation: The Digital Services Act (2022) establishes a new framework for online intermediary services. It introduces graduated obligations based on platform size, including enhanced duties for very large online platforms (VLOPs) on content moderation, transparency, and algorithmic accountability.

text: Which EU regulation targets 'gatekeeper' digital platforms to ensure fair market access?
explanation: The Digital Markets Act (DMA, 2022) designates certain large online platforms as 'gatekeepers' and imposes ex-ante obligations to ensure contestable and fair digital markets. Gatekeepers include search engines, app stores, and social networks meeting specific thresholds.

text: In which year did the GDPR become applicable?
explanation: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, Regulation 2016/679) was adopted in April 2016 but became applicable on 25 May 2018, giving organisations two years to comply. It applies to all organisations processing EU residents' personal data.

text: Which EU regulation determines which Member State is responsible for examining an asylum application?
explanation: The Dublin Regulation (currently Dublin III, 2013) establishes the criteria for determining which Member State is responsible for an asylum application. The general principle is that the first EU country of entry is responsible, which puts disproportionate pressure on border states.

text: In which year did the Schengen Agreement enter into force, abolishing border controls?
explanation: The Schengen Agreement was signed in 1985 and the implementing Convention in 1990, but the abolition of internal border controls began in 1995 for the first group of five states (France, Germany, Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg). The Schengen acquis was integrated into EU law by the Amsterdam Treaty.

text: How many countries are currently members of the Schengen Area?
explanation: As of 2024, the Schengen Area has 29 members — 25 EU Member States (Ireland and Cyprus are not full members) plus Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland. Bulgaria and Romania fully joined in 2024 (air/sea borders March 2024, land borders January 2024).

text: Which EU agency is responsible for managing the external borders of the Schengen Area?
explanation: Frontex (European Border and Coast Guard Agency) manages and coordinates EU external border surveillance. It was significantly reinforced in 2019 with a mandate for a standing corps of 10,000 border guards and broadened return powers.

text: Which EU agency is responsible for evaluating and approving medicines for the EU market?
explanation: The European Medicines Agency (EMA), now headquartered in Amsterdam, evaluates and supervises medicines for the EU. It moved from London following Brexit. EFSA covers food safety, ECDC covers disease prevention, and EEA covers environment.

text: What is the primary mandate of Europol?
options: Border surveillance at EU external frontiers
Prosecution of EU budget fraud cases
Facilitating law enforcement cooperation against serious crime
Judicial cooperation in cross-border criminal proceedings
explanation: Europol (headquartered in The Hague) supports and strengthens cooperation between national law enforcement authorities in fighting serious organised crime, terrorism and cybercrime. Unlike the European Public Prosecutor's Office, it has no executive powers of arrest.

text: Who holds the post of EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy?
options: A dual-hatted VP of the Commission and chair of the FAC
explanation: The HR/VP post was created by the Lisbon Treaty: it combines the roles of Vice-President of the European Commission and chair of the Foreign Affairs Council. Kaja Kallas holds this position since December 2024.

text: Which EU defence cooperation framework was activated in 2017 under Article 46 TEU?
explanation: PESCO (Permanent Structured Cooperation), established by Council Decision in December 2017, is a framework within the EU's defence policy allowing 25 participating Member States to deepen defence cooperation and develop joint military capabilities.

text: What is the 'Strategic Compass' adopted by the EU in 2022?
options: A common EU defence treaty replacing NATO
The EU's strategic framework on security and defence to 2030
An EU diplomatic strategy for the Eastern neighbourhood
A rotating EU military command framework
explanation: The Strategic Compass (March 2022) is the EU's strategic framework on security and defence to 2030. It sets concrete goals including a Rapid Deployment Capacity of 5,000 troops, enhanced cyber defence, space capabilities, and hybrid threat resilience.

text: Which body constitutes the EU's diplomatic service?
explanation: The European External Action Service (EEAS), established by the Lisbon Treaty, is the EU's diplomatic corps. It operates under the authority of the HR/VP, manages EU Delegations worldwide (over 140), and supports EU external action.

text: What status does the EU hold at the United Nations General Assembly?
explanation: The EU has enhanced observer status at the UN General Assembly (since 2011), allowing it to speak on behalf of its Member States. It is not a UN member and cannot vote. France and Germany hold permanent and non-permanent Council seats respectively among Member States.

text: When were Ukraine and Moldova granted EU candidate status?
explanation: The European Council of 23 June 2022 granted candidate status to Ukraine and Moldova. Accession negotiations were formally opened in June 2024. Georgia received the status of potential candidate at the same time and was upgraded to candidate in December 2023.

text: What are the 'Copenhagen Criteria' for EU accession?
options: Economic convergence criteria from the Maastricht Treaty
Political, economic and institutional conditions for candidate countries
Schengen security standards for border management
Environmental standards for the Green Deal
explanation: The Copenhagen Criteria (1993) define the conditions for EU membership: (1) stable institutions guaranteeing democracy, rule of law and human rights; (2) a functioning market economy; (3) ability to take on the obligations of membership including the acquis communautaire.

text: What right does EU citizenship grant regarding elections in another Member State?
options: Right to vote in national parliamentary elections
Right to vote in European and municipal elections
Right to vote in all elections including referenda
Right to stand in all elections after 5 years
explanation: EU citizens residing in another Member State have the right to vote and stand as candidates in European Parliament elections and in local (municipal) elections in their Member State of residence (Article 22 TFEU). They do not have the right to vote in national parliamentary elections.

text: How many citizens from at least how many Member States are needed for a European Citizens' Initiative?
options: 500,000 citizens from at least 5 Member States
1 million citizens from at least one quarter of Member States
1 million citizens from at least half of Member States
500,000 citizens from at least 7 Member States
explanation: A European Citizens' Initiative (ECI) requires signatures from at least 1 million EU citizens from at least 7 Member States (one quarter of 27). It allows citizens to invite the Commission to propose legislation on matters within its competence.

text: When did the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights become legally binding?
options: 2000, when it was proclaimed in Nice
explanation: The EU Charter of Fundamental Rights was proclaimed in Nice in 2000, but only acquired legally binding status on 1 December 2009 with the entry into force of the Treaty of Lisbon (Article 6 TEU). It now has the same legal value as the Treaties.

text: Which procedure under Article 7 TEU can lead to the suspension of a Member State's voting rights?
explanation: Article 7 TEU allows the Council to determine a 'clear risk of a serious breach' of EU values (4/5 majority), and the European Council to determine a 'serious and persistent breach' (unanimity). The Council may then suspend rights including voting rights. Procedures were opened against Poland (2017) and Hungary (2018).

text: In which year was the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) launched?
explanation: The CAP was launched in 1962, implementing the agricultural provisions of the 1957 Treaty of Rome. It initially focused on guaranteed prices and production subsidies to ensure food security. The current CAP covers 2023–2027.

text: What do the two pillars of the CAP cover?
options: Direct payments to farmers and rural development
EU internal market and EU export subsidies
explanation: The CAP's Pillar 1 covers direct payments to farmers and market measures (funded entirely by the EU). Pillar 2 covers rural development programmes (co-financed by Member States). Pillar 1 absorbs more than two-thirds of the CAP budget.

text: Which body negotiates international trade agreements on behalf of the EU?
explanation: The European Commission negotiates trade agreements on behalf of the EU, based on a mandate approved by the Council. The Council must authorise the opening of negotiations and approve the final agreement. The European Parliament must give its consent for the agreement to enter into force.

text: Which EU body directly supervises significant banks in the euro area under the SSM?
explanation: Under the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM, established 2014), the ECB directly supervises significant banks in the euro area (those meeting certain size or cross-border thresholds, approximately 110 banks). National supervisors continue to oversee less significant institutions.

text: Which EU fund supports employment, social inclusion and education through the Cohesion Policy?
explanation: The European Social Fund+ (ESF+) is the EU's main instrument for investing in people: employment, education, training, and social inclusion. The ERDF funds infrastructure and innovation, the Cohesion Fund supports transport and environment in less developed Member States.

text: What is the EU's framework programme for research and innovation for 2021–2027?
explanation: Horizon Europe (2021–2027) is the EU's flagship research and innovation programme, with a budget of €95.5 billion. It succeeds Horizon 2020 and includes the European Research Council, Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions, and research missions on cancer, climate, oceans, cities and soil.

text: What is the EU programme for education, training, youth and sport?
explanation: Erasmus+ is the EU programme supporting education, training, youth and sport. For 2021–2027, it has a budget of approximately €26.2 billion. Since 1987, it has supported the mobility of over 12 million students and staff.

text: What is the EU's satellite navigation system?
explanation: Galileo is the EU's own global satellite navigation system, providing positioning and timing services worldwide. It became fully operational in 2016. Copernicus is the EU's Earth observation programme — a different system. GPS is American and GLONASS is Russian.

text: What is the Copernicus programme?
explanation: Copernicus is the EU's Earth observation programme, providing free and open data on land, marine environment, atmosphere, climate change, emergency management and security. It is managed by the European Commission in partnership with ESA and EUMETSAT.

text: Which EU institution hosts the Transparency Register for lobby organisations?
explanation: The EU Transparency Register is a joint register of the European Parliament, Council and Commission (since 2021), listing organisations seeking to influence EU decision-making. Registration has been made mandatory for meeting with senior officials of the Commission, Parliament rapporteurs and Council Presidency.

text: What body handles complaints about maladministration in EU institutions?
explanation: The European Ombudsman investigates complaints about maladministration by EU institutions, bodies, offices and agencies. The Ombudsman is elected by the European Parliament. Citizens, residents and companies registered in the EU can submit complaints.

text: What is OLAF's main function?
options: Judicial prosecution of EU budget fraud
Administrative investigation of fraud against EU
Supervision of EU officials' financial declarations
explanation: OLAF (European Anti-Fraud Office) conducts independent administrative investigations to protect EU finances against fraud, corruption and serious misconduct. Unlike the European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO), OLAF cannot directly prosecute — it issues recommendations to national authorities.

text: The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) can directly prosecute which type of offences?
explanation: The EPPO, operational since June 2021 and based in Luxembourg (with 22 participating Member States), has exclusive competence to investigate and prosecute crimes affecting the EU's financial interests, including VAT fraud, corruption and misuse of EU funds.

text: What is the official motto of the European Union?
explanation: 'United in diversity' is the EU's official motto, adopted in 2000 following a selection process. It reflects that Europeans are united in their common project of peace and prosperity, while drawing strength from the continent's many different cultures, traditions and languages.

text: Which musical work is used as the EU's anthem?
explanation: The EU anthem is the 'Ode to Joy', the prelude to the fourth movement of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony, arranged by Herbert von Karajan. Adopted by the Council of Europe in 1972 and by the EU in 1985, it is performed without words to transcend language barriers.

text: In which year were the first direct elections to the European Parliament held?
explanation: The first direct elections to the European Parliament took place in June 1979. Simone Veil was elected as its first President. Before 1979, MEPs were appointed by national parliaments.

text: How many principles does the European Pillar of Social Rights consist of?
explanation: The European Pillar of Social Rights, proclaimed in 2017 at the Gothenburg Social Summit, contains 20 principles covering three chapters: equal opportunities and access to the labour market, fair working conditions, and social protection and inclusion.

text: What is the EU's annual research and development fund for defence?
explanation: The European Defence Fund (EDF), with a budget of €7.95 billion for 2021–2027, is the first EU budget instrument to directly fund collaborative defence research and capability development projects. It supports research and industrial development phases.

text: What is the minimum number of Member States required to establish enhanced cooperation?
explanation: Enhanced cooperation (Article 20 TEU) requires a minimum of 9 Member States. It allows a group of willing Member States to proceed with closer integration in areas where unanimous agreement cannot be reached. It has been used for the unitary patent, divorce law, and the EPPO.
